title: Peter walks on water (Matthew 14:22–33)
hook: Peter steps out, looks at the wind, sinks, and is caught by the hand
tomorrow: Who do you say I am?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the storm: a sleeping teacher, a shout, and peace, be still. What storm did you name? Today closes week eight, and the road through Galilee. One more night on the lake. Day fifty-six.

The first day of a new job. Asking someone out. Standing up to speak. There's a moment where a person either steps out or doesn't. Back to the lake, the same night as the boy's lunch. Jesus sends the disciples ahead in the boat and goes up a mountain alone to pray. Out on the water the wind is against them, and the waves toss the boat. Then, Matthew says, in the fourth watch of the night, the last stretch before dawn, they see him coming toward them, walking on the sea. They scream. They think it's a ghost. Today, oligopistos.
screen: `THE MOMENT BEFORE YOU STEP OUT.` → `THE FOURTH WATCH OF THE NIGHT.` → `A FIGURE WALKING ON THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Straightaway he speaks, in the King James Bible: "Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid." And Peter, of course it's Peter, answers: "Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water." One word comes back: come. And Peter climbs over the side. He actually walks. Then: "But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me." That's the whole shape of the story. He steps out. He looks at the wind instead of the one he's walking toward. He sinks. A prayer of three words: Lord, save me. No time for more. And then: "And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?" Immediately. Not after a lesson. The hand comes first, and the question after. Little faith, in Matthew's Greek, is one word, oligopistos. It's almost a nickname. Matthew's Jesus uses it for his disciples more than once. Little faith. Not no faith. Enough to step out, not quite enough to keep looking up. And when they climb back in, the wind stops, and the people in the boat worship him and say, of a truth thou art the Son of God. That's where these two weeks on the road through Galilee end. Stargazers, a family fleeing, a boy asking questions, a wild man, a river, a desert, full nets, a party, a wedding, a well, a lunch, a storm. And now a man sinking, and a hand.
screen: `BE OF GOOD CHEER; IT IS I.` · `BID ME COME UNTO THEE.` · `HE SAW THE WIND, AND SANK.` · `LITTLE FAITH, NOT NO FAITH.` · then, large: `LORD, SAVE ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and feel your weight in the chair. Think of one step you've been waiting to feel ready for. A call, an application, an apology, a hard conversation, a first try at something. Picture yourself taking it. Not the whole journey, just the first step over the side. Notice where your eyes go. To the wind? To what could go wrong? Then remember the hand in the story, which came immediately. If you pray, you can use Peter's three words. The bell holds the time.

Oligopistos. One Greek word for you of little faith, Jesus's nickname for Peter after he stepped out and began to sink. These two weeks' words: the magi, the Holy Innocents, baptism, disciple, semeion, the Samaritan woman, the storm.
Your line: he catches the sinking. Today, take one step before you feel ready. Tomorrow the road turns toward Jerusalem, with a question. Day fifty-six.

screen: `DAY 56 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO DO YOU SAY I AM?`

howItsDone: Many Christians pray Peter's words, Lord, save me, in moments of fear, and the story is often preached on trust and doubt. Icons and paintings of the scene show Christ's hand reaching for Peter as he sinks.

original.note: Greek: you of little faith. One word, almost a nickname, that Jesus uses for his disciples more than once in Matthew.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle about walking on water.
what it means: a man steps out, looks at the wind, sinks, and is caught by the hand before he's given a lesson.
what a scholar hears: oligopistos, little faith, is a word Matthew's Jesus keeps for his own disciples, and his it is I, ego eimi, can also be heard as I am, the name God gives at the burning bush.

notes: Week-end and part close: the teach and word look back over 'The road through Galilee' (days 44–56); the carry points to day 57 and the Jerusalem part.
The script calls this 'the same night as the boy's lunch' (Matthew 14:22 follows the feeding directly; John 6:16–21 also places the walking on water after it). Day 54 used John's feeding account.
Fourth watch (Roman reckoning) about 3–6 a.m.; confirm.
'One of the shortest prayers in the Gospels' for 'Lord, save me'; confirm.
Ego eimi as an echo of Exodus 3:14 (LXX ego eimi ho on) is a common scholarly observation; stated as 'can also be heard as'.
